newsitem.title: USA: Soybean prices soar, coffee and oil lower.
newsitem.headline: Soybean prices soar, coffee and oil lower.

text.p: Soybean futures soared on Friday on rumors that China was buying from the United States and further drawing down already low stockpiles.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans for May delivery closed 20-3/4 cents a bushel higher at $8.67-3/4.

"The talk of the Chinese interest in the U.S. beans gave the funds a reason to reload long positions," said John Kleist, director of agricultural research for ING Futures and Options, referring to speculative commodity fund investors.

The buying was tied to reports that China had bought at least one cargo of U.S. soybeans on Thursday night. The buying, though small, reminded traders of the tightrope now being walked by soybean customers.

Demand from processors, who crush soybeans into meal for animal feed and oils for industrial or food use, has been running at record levels most of the winter. Soybean exports, meanwhile, have also been running 15 percent ahead of last year.
"That's in the trade's mind now," said Dave Armstrong, analyst with ABN-AMRO Chicago Corp, referring to ideas nearby demand remained too strong for remaining soybean supplies.

"The signs are the big March crush that was reported yesterday, less slowdown than people were calling for in the weekly crush, strong basis (cash prices) in the eastern Corn Belt and continued strong export sales," Armstrong said.
The U.S. Census Bureau on Thursday said soybean crushing in March reached 130 million bushels, up from 125 million in February and compared to 115 million crushed in March 1996.
The Agriculture Department earlier this month cut its estimate of U.S. soybean stocks next September to 125 million bushels, down from 183 million a year earlier.
Buoyed by soybeans, soymeal for May delivery closed at $281.60 a ton, up $8.60 or just below the daily allowable rise of $10 a ton.

Corn prices benefited from the gains in soybeans and from fresh export demand. But cool, clear planting weather in the Midwest lent optimism about coming supplies. May corn closed up 1-1/2 cents a bushel at $2.94-1/2.

Wheat prices also closed higher on renewed concerns about harsh weather in Texas and Oklahoma hurting winter wheat already damged by last week's hard freeze. Wheat for May delivery traded in Chicago closed up 2 cents a bushel at $4.23-1/2.
Support also came from belief that more rain is needed in dry European areas to stem further deterioration of wheat there.
"They're going to get some rain in Europe but they need a lot more, and there's a lot of rain in the Panhandle of Texas and in Oklahoma," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter.

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee prices closed lower on news that a six-day truckers' strike in Colombia had ended. Coffee for May delivery closed 3.40 cents a pound lower at 216.35 cents.
"They settled the strike in Colombia, so the market's giving back some of what it has gained on that news," said Smith Barney analyst Walt Spilka.

Strikes in Colombia, the number two coffee exporter, had earlier contributed to a doubling in coffee prices between December and March. Analysts said coffee stockpiles at roasters remain historically low, so prices may stay firm.
"The end of the Colombia strike really should not matter," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "There are so many other bullish fundamental factors."

Those factors include a voluntary scheme of export quotas among coffee producing nations as well as speculation that this year's crop in Brazil, the top producer, may come in much smaller than expected.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices closed mostly lower after Nigeria's state oil company said ethnic clashes that have disrupted some production there would only delay, not prevent, exports of crude oil.
Crude for June delivery closed down 4 cents at $19.99 a barrel, May gasoline down 0.34 cent a gallon at 62.50 cents and May heating oil up 0.01 cent a gallon at 55.90 cents.

Royal Dutch/Shell Group said earlier this week that clashes among the Ijaw and Itsekiri tribes in Nigeria forced it to close its Warri flow station last weekend. On Friday Shell said it had cut Nigerian output by about 90,000 barrels a day.
But the Nigerian National Petroleum Corp also said that no oil exports would be cancelled, although loadings had been delayed two to three days.
"Crude went up on the Shell news, which I think was pretty bullish, but traders still took their profits," said Al Lindseth, manager of oil and gas hedge programs at GSC Energy in Atlanta.
